title: Life Skills Shorts · Episode 2
chapters: Small talk that isn't so small
Switching providers: beating the loyalty tax
The emergency department: how it really works

units.t: Life Skills Shorts. Episode two.
In this episode: Small talk that isn't so small, Switching providers: beating the loyalty tax, The emergency department: how it really works and Travelling overseas without the drama.
Part one. Small talk that isn't so small.
Most of us avoid chatting with strangers because we expect it to be awkward.
Experiments suggest we have badly misjudged both them and ourselves.
We misjudge strangers.
In a 2014 study, psychologists Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder asked Chicago train and bus commuters to talk to a stranger, keep to themselves or commute as usual.
Beforehand, people predicted talking would be the least pleasant.
Afterwards, those who chatted reported the most positive journeys.
Those approached were generally happy to talk.
The effects were modest, not life-changing.
A 2018 study led by Erica Boothby found the liking gap: after chatting, people underestimated how much their partner liked them.
We replay our own awkward moments, while the other person just found us pleasant.
The gap appeared in labs, among university housemates and in public workshops.
If you leave thinking you were boring, they very probably did not.
Why weak ties matter.
Close friends and family are central to wellbeing, but casual connections count too.
Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn found that people felt happier on days with more interactions with weak ties, such as classmates, neighbours and the person who makes their coffee.
In another study, customers asked to have a genuine, friendly exchange with a barista left in a better mood than those told to be efficient.
Weak ties also bring practical benefits.

Mark Granovetter's classic research suggested that new opportunities, including jobs, often come through acquaintances rather than close friends, because they move in different circles and hear about different things.
Openers and follow-ups.
Most people overthink the first sentence.
You need a door, not wit.
Comment on your shared situation: the weather, the queue, the food.
‘Have you been to one of these before?’
works at most gatherings.
Open questions give the other person room to talk.
A popular memory aid is FORD: family, occupation, recreation and dreams.
Read the cues, though: someone with headphones on and eyes on a book may not want company.
A 2017 Harvard study led by Karen Huang analysed real conversations, including online chats and speed dating.
People who asked more questions were better liked, and follow-up questions mattered most.
If someone mentions Tasmania, ‘What was the highlight?’
shows you heard them, which switching to your own holiday does not.
People tend to ask fewer questions than ideal.
Going a little deeper.
Small talk is a warm-up, not a destination.

Research by Michael Kardas, Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, published in 2022, found that people expected deep conversations with strangers to feel more awkward and less enjoyable than they actually were.
Participants who answered more personal, meaningful questions consistently felt more connected than they had predicted.
You do not need to leap to intimate subjects.
Moving from ‘What do you do?’
to ‘What do you enjoy most about it?’
or ‘How did you end up doing that?’
invites a real answer.
Offering something genuine about yourself in return helps the other person feel safe going further.
Ending well.
Ending a conversation can feel harder than starting one.
A 2021 study led by Adam Mastroianni asked people how long they had wanted their conversations to last.
Conversations almost never ended when both people wanted them to.
Often both wanted to stop earlier, or one wanted more and the other less, and neither could tell.
So a graceful exit helps.
Summarise something from the chat, thank them and give a reason, even a simple one: ‘I'll let you get back to your evening.
It was great hearing about the trip.’
If you would like to meet again, say so specifically.
A clean, warm ending leaves both people with a good final impression.
The key idea: We expect talking to strangers to be unpleasant and underestimate how much they like us, and we are wrong on both counts.
Part two. Switching providers: beating the loyalty tax.
Staying with the same provider for years can quietly cost you.
A little comparison, a phone call and a calendar reminder can trim your household bills without changing how you live.
The loyalty tax.
Picture two neighbours with identical houses and habits.
One signed up with an energy retailer a decade ago and never looked again.
The other compares plans each year.
The first often pays noticeably more, because a discount expired or cheaper plans arrived that they never moved to.
This pattern, sometimes called the loyalty tax, shows up across energy, phone, internet and insurance.
Providers rely on inertia.
The fix is not constant switching.
Choose one month, perhaps around tax time, and review every regular bill in a single sitting.
Start with your latest bills: usage, daily supply charge, rates, any time-of-use pricing and your solar feed-in tariff.
Compare energy officially.
For electricity and gas, use free government comparison sites rather than commercial ones that may be paid by retailers.
In New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania and the ACT, the Australian Energy Regulator runs Energy Made Easy at energymadeeasy.
gov.
au.
In Victoria, use Victorian Energy Compare.
Western Australia and the Northern Territory have different market arrangements, with fewer choices in many areas.
Enter your usage or upload a bill to see plans at your address.
In many states retailers must show how offers compare with a government reference price.
Look past headline discounts: conditional discounts that vanish if you pay late can make a plan dearer than it looks.
Switching and right-sizing.
Changing energy retailers usually involves no physical work.
The same poles, wires and meter supply you, and only the company billing you changes.
The new retailer arranges the transfer.
Check for exit fees and contract end dates.
You can usually keep your mobile number, and month-to-month plans leave you free to go.
Sometimes just telling your provider you are thinking of leaving gets you a better plan.
Many people pay for more mobile data or home internet speed than they use.
Check your usage in your provider's app, then choose a plan with a modest buffer.
On the NBN, typical evening speeds matter more than maximums.
Cancel streaming services and subscriptions you no longer use.
Hardship help.
If paying bills is becoming hard, act before disconnection notices arrive.
Energy retailers must have hardship programs, which can include payment plans, advice on cutting usage and protection from disconnection while you take part.
Telcos have financial hardship policies too.
Ask for the hardship team by name.
State and territory governments offer energy concessions and rebates to eligible people, such as pensioners, healthcare card holders and some low-income households.
These are not always applied automatically, so check your state government's website.
Services Australia can tell you which cards and payments you may qualify for.
The free National Debt Helpline, on 1800 007 007, connects you with a financial counsellor who can negotiate with providers for you.
When things go wrong.
Billing errors, surprise fees and botched transfers do happen.
Contact the provider, explain the problem clearly and ask for a complaint reference number.
Keep notes of every call, including the date and the name of the person you spoke with.
If the problem isn't fixed, you can go to an independent ombudsman for free.
For phone and internet, that is the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman.
For energy and water, most states have their own energy and water ombudsman scheme, so check which applies in your state.
Ombudsmen can investigate and, in many cases, require providers to fix the problem or pay compensation.
This is general information; check moneysmart.
gov.
au and your state's consumer affairs website.
The key idea: Long-term customers often pay more than new ones, so check your deals once a year.
Part three. The emergency department: how it really works.
Why does someone who arrived after you get seen first?
The answer goes back to Napoleon's battlefields, and understanding it makes a hospital visit far less frustrating.
Born on the battlefield.
For much of history, wounded soldiers were treated according to rank, or not until the fighting ended.
Dominique-Jean Larrey, a surgeon in Napoleon's armies, changed that.
He introduced light, fast horse-drawn ‘flying ambulances’ to reach the wounded during battle, and insisted the most dangerously injured be treated first, whatever their rank or even their side.
The word triage comes from the French trier, meaning to sort.
The idea spread through military medicine and, in the twentieth century, into civilian hospitals.
The principle is the same today.
An emergency department is not a queue.
It is a sorting system designed to make sure the person most likely to die without help is seen first.
Triage and the scale.
At an Australian emergency department you will usually speak first with a triage nurse.
In a couple of minutes they ask what has happened, check key signs such as breathing and pulse, and look for danger.
They are not diagnosing you.
They are deciding how long you can safely wait.
Be clear and specific, and neither exaggerate nor play things down.
Australian and New Zealand departments use the Australasian Triage Scale, in place in various forms since the 1990s.
Category 1 is immediately life-threatening, seen immediately.
Category 2, such as severe chest pain, within 10 minutes.
Category 3 within 30 minutes, Category 4 within an hour and Category 5 within two hours.
These are the maximum times for assessment and treatment to begin, not for the whole visit.
Busy departments sometimes miss targets.
Why you might wait.
Waiting rooms can be maddening, especially when others are called ahead of you.
Usually someone more urgent has come in, perhaps by ambulance through a different door.
Arriving by ambulance does not jump the queue.
Ambulance patients are triaged too, so a less urgent one may still wait.
Another major cause of delay is access block.
When patients who need admission cannot move to a ward because no beds are free, they stay in emergency, occupying cubicles and staff time.
That is why waits often reflect pressure across the whole hospital rather than slow work in the department itself.
Choosing, and preparing.

Always call Triple Zero, 000, or go to emergency for chest pain, difficulty breathing, signs of stroke such as a drooping face or slurred speech, severe bleeding, a serious head injury, seizures, severe burns, or someone unconscious or unresponsive.
If in doubt, call 000.
For a sprain, minor cut or ear infection, a GP, after-hours GP or urgent care clinic may see you faster, and pharmacists and nurse-staffed advice lines can help you decide.
If you go, bring your Medicare card, a list of medicines and allergies, and details of your doctor.
Ask staff before you eat or drink, as you may need surgery or tests.
A friend can listen and speak up for you.
If your condition worsens while you wait, tell the triage nurse straight away.
You can be reassessed and moved up.
Costs and afterwards.
If you are eligible for Medicare, treatment as a public patient in a public hospital emergency department costs nothing.
Ambulances are different.
Some states and territories cover their own residents, while others can charge substantial fees unless you have ambulance cover through a state scheme or private health insurance.
Check your situation before you need one, though cost should never stop you calling 000 in an emergency.
When you are discharged, ask for a copy of your discharge summary, make sure you understand any new medicines and warning signs, and book a follow-up with your GP.
The emergency department fixes the crisis.
Your GP handles what comes after.
The key idea: Triage means treating the sickest first, an idea that began in Napoleonic battlefield medicine.
Part four. Travelling overseas without the drama.
The best trips start long before the airport.
A little preparation with your passport, the right insurance and official travel advice can save you a world of trouble.
Passport and entry rules.
Every year some travellers are turned away at check-in because their passport expires too soon.
Many countries require it to be valid for at least six months beyond your arrival or departure date, and some need blank pages.
Check the expiry date months ahead and renew at passports.
gov.
au.
Processing times can stretch in busy seasons, and priority processing costs extra.
Australians can visit many countries without a visa, but not all.
Some require an electronic authorisation applied for online, such as the US ESTA or UK ETA; others need an embassy visa.
Do not forget countries where you only change planes.
Use official government sites linked from Smartraveller, and beware look-alike sites charging large fees for forms you could lodge yourself.
Some common medicines are restricted overseas, so check those rules too.
Smartraveller and insurance.
Smartraveller, smartraveller.
gov.
au, run by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, gives each destination an advice level, from 'Exercise normal safety precautions' up to 'Do not travel'.
Regions can differ.
Read it before you book and again before you leave.
Insurers may refuse cover in places marked 'Do not travel'.
Smartraveller puts it bluntly: if you cannot afford travel insurance, you cannot afford to travel.
Overseas treatment can cost tens of thousands of dollars, and an evacuation flight home far more.

Buy cover when you book so cancellation is protected, then read the product disclosure statement for pre-existing conditions, the excess, and exclusions such as scooter riding without the right licence, extreme sports or alcohol.
Credit card insurance often has strict conditions.
Money, phones, documents.
A card blocked for suspicious overseas activity can leave you stranded at a hotel desk.
Check whether your bank wants to know your travel plans, and carry at least two ways to pay, kept in different places.
Compare fees: some cards charge international transaction fees on every purchase, while travel cards and some bank accounts do not.
Before you leave, check your phone plan's roaming charges, which can be huge, or plan to buy a local SIM or eSIM.
Save digital copies of your passport, insurance policy and bookings somewhere you can reach from any device, and share them with someone at home.
A printed copy of your insurer's emergency number in your wallet is a smart backup.
Your health on the road.
Some vaccinations need several weeks to take effect, or more than one dose, so book a GP or travel clinic six to eight weeks before departure if you can.
Bring a list of your medicines and a letter from your doctor describing them, and keep them in original labelled packaging.
Australia has reciprocal health care agreements with some countries, including the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Ireland.
These can cover medically necessary treatment, but they are limited and do not replace insurance.
On long flights, move around and drink water.
Healthdirect and Smartraveller both have practical travel health pages.
This is general information, not medical advice, so talk to a health professional about your own needs.
When things go wrong.
If your passport is stolen, report it to local police and contact the nearest Australian embassy or consulate for an emergency travel document.
If you are arrested, seriously ill or caught in a crisis, consular staff can help, and the 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre can be reached from anywhere.
Smartraveller lists the numbers.
But the Consular Services Charter is clear about the limits.
The government cannot pay your medical bills or legal fees, get you out of jail or override local laws.
That is exactly why insurance and good preparation matter.
Before you leave, make sure someone at home has your itinerary and knows how to reach you, and check in with them regularly.
The key idea: Check your passport expiry months ahead, as many countries want six months' validity, and check entry rules for every country, including transits.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is the ‘liking gap’?
Answer. People underrate how much others like them.
Question two. What does the 'loyalty tax' refer to?
Answer. Loyal customers often paying more than new ones.
Question three. What principle does triage follow?
Answer. The sickest patients are seen first.
Question four. Why check your passport expiry date months before travelling?
Answer. Many countries want six months' validity beyond your trip.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
